html:
Greek fire was a burning liquid weapon used by the Byzantine Empire from the 670s. Sailors sprayed it from siphons, pumped tubes on the bows of their ships, and it kept burning on water.

Byzantine writers credit Kallinikos, an architect who fled from Syria, with bringing it to Constantinople around 672. It soon proved itself against Arab fleets in the first Arab siege and again in the second in 717 and 718. In 941 it burned much of the fleet of the Rus' prince Igor of Kiev.

The recipe was a state secret, known to a few people, and it is now lost. Most scholars think it was based on crude oil from around the Black Sea, mixed with resins, something like napalm. Its fame grew so large that Western writers later called many kinds of fire weapons "Greek fire".
sum: Greek fire was a burning liquid weapon used by the Byzantine Empire from the 670s. Sailors sprayed it from siphons, pumped tubes on the bows of their ships, and it kept burning on water.
